Thanks for raising this. It's unfortunately a very tricky one to deal with directly in a clean and widely-supportable manner, so there might not be a great out-of-the-box option. It's a reasonable use case, but also an uncommon-enough one that it wouldn't be enough to drive a big change across the ecosystem, which is what message template syntax and semantic changes tend to entail.

Since the problem is fundamentally a rendering issue, though, the first place I'd look for a workable solution is _Serilog.Expressions_, which is a Swiss Army knife for hacking in modifications to rendering of all sorts. You can plug in custom functions (https://github.com/serilog/serilog-expressions/?tab=readme-ov-file#implementing-user-defined-functions) that get full access to the underlying `LogEvent` and its message template, including the raw text, and you can parameterize them either via the call syntax in your output template, or at configuration time when you plug them in.

It might not be a simple matter to get _Expressions_ wired in between Serilog and your sink of choice, but worth taking a look at, anyway.

Hi @slepmog,

`@p['some name']` is only required (in expression templates) if a property has a non-identifier name in its path. You can refer to structured object sub-properties in expression templates using regular dotted syntax, e.g. `ThatObject.ImportantProperty`.

Expression templates (per logger) are different from message templates (per event). Message templates are super-simple and drive capturing the data as well as formatting it. Expression templates are much more sophisticated, but only usable for formatting.

HTH!

comments.body:
Not really a solution, but probably worth mentioning if you don't know about it ... 

In some project we are currently using [`Elastic.CommonSchema.Serilog`](https://github.com/elastic/ecs-dotnet/tree/main/src/Elastic.CommonSchema.Serilog) ... what it does is that we write logs however we want in the app ... but "some" property names are recognized [and get mapped to the corresponding "standard" in the ECS Schema](Elastic.CommonSchema.LogTemplateProperties) ... and the ECS schema, while not identical, is [fairly close to OTel Semantic Conventions](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/ecs/ecs-otel-alignment-details).

What we end up doing is that: 
- in "generic" logging enrichment portions (think "Middleware that enriches from incoming HTTP requests") we use ECS standard properties, for instance using constants exposed in [`Elastic.CommonSchema.LogTemplateProperties`](https://github.com/elastic/ecs-dotnet/blob/main/src/Elastic.CommonSchema/LogTemplateProperties.Generated.cs) ... 

code looks like : 

```cs
   _logger.ForContext(Elastic.CommonSchema.LogTemplateProperties.UserId, "userId").Information(....);

  // or 
  
  `_diagnosticContext.Set(Elastic.CommonSchema.LogTemplateProperties.UserId, "userId")
```

- in specific logging, if we have access to data that seem to match ECS reference, we enrich the context with properties from  `Elastic.CommonSchema.LogTemplateProperties` , using `LogContext` or "contextual loggers"


The caveat is that the ECS Serilog library does the mapping from those "well known properties" to the expected naming in the JSON Logs as part of Formatting, i.e. when "spitting out" the logs, not where they are written.

comments.body:
Hi!

Serilog's built-in `IBatchedLogEventSink` support does support this functionality, and includes test suite entries that cover it.

Although _Serilog.Sinks.AwsCloudWatch_ is uses recent APIs, it [has dependencies on old versions](https://www.nuget.org/packages/serilog.sinks.awscloudwatch) of the packages involved (probably to maximise backwards compatibility). NuGet's default package installation algorithm resolves dependencies to the minimum, rather than maximum, version that can support the other packages in your solution.

To make sure your app actually uses the latest functionality, your best bets are:

 * Add an explicit reference to version 5.0.0 of _Serilog.Sinks.PeriodicBatching_, or
 * Update _Serilog.Sinks.AwsCloudWatch_ to remove the _Serilog.Sinks.PeriodicBatching_ dependency, using the built-in _Serilog_ package's batching features directly.

Hope this helps,

Nick

Hey Nick, thanks so much for this package and for taking the time to respond.

Your explanation makes sense and I'm adding `Serilog.Sinks.PeriodicBatching` as a top-level dependency so I can specifically install the latest version, but I still have a question about how to actually use the `PeriodicBatchingSink.EmitAsync()` from the consumer-side of things.

I'm assuming that what left unsaid in your response is that a call to `logger.Dispose()` will automatically emit the batched log events after upgrading to `PeriodicBatching` 5.x?

Do you mind clarifying when/where the call to `EmitAsync()` is being made? `CloudWatchLogSink` instantiates a `PeriodicBatchingSink` with an inner `PeriodicBatchingSinkImplementationCallback` implementing `IBatchedLogEventSink`, but neither `PeriodicBatchingSink` doesn't call `EmitBatch()`/`EmitBatchAsync()` in its `Dispose()` implementation and the other nuget's `PeriodicBatchingSinkImplementationCallback` isn't even disposable. I see that a `DisposingAggregateSink` gets created from the `CreateSink` call, but that's not aware of `IBatchedLogEventSink` (so far as I can tell).

Separately, as the `PeriodicBatchingSink` instance is private (via composition) to `CloudWatchLogSink` (and `CloudWatchLogSink` doesn't implement `IBatchedLogEventSink` itself), I think the other part of my question about flushing all sinks *without* disposing the logger is still not possible? Even if/when `CloudWatchLogSink` skips the intermediary `PeriodicBatching` crate and directly using the batching APIs in newer serilog versions, Serilog doesn't really provide access to a logger instance's sinks (because they're treated as immutable) so there's no convenient way to call `EmitBatchAsync()` externally without bypassing the easy-to-use static `LoggerConfiguration` extension methods and creating your own instance of `XxxSink` then storing it *somewhere* so you can manually call `EmitBatchAsync()` (or its native serilog alternative?) when and where needed?

I really appreciate your help and patience, sorry for asking all these questions but despite using Serilog for probably over a decade this is the first time I've had to dive into its internals.

Thanks for your reply, Mahmoud.

Just to answer your second question, which I skipped earlier - there's no API for manually flushing a batched sink in Serilog, as things stand. It's been considered a few times in the past but hasn't seemed worth the added complexity, for the scenarios it would cover.

The latest `Serilog.Sinks.PeriodicBatching` package is a fairly complex compatibility shim to keep the ecosystem working, but there's probably not much point digging into its internals here. For a maintained sink like the CloudWatch one, switching over to use the newer Serilog functionality directly will be a better bet for the long haul.

The new batching sink is this one:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Core/Sinks/Batching/BatchingSink.cs

Its dispose methods signal to the background task that shutdown is required, and then wait on the background task to complete:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Core/Sinks/Batching/BatchingSink.cs#L263

The task itself, after observing cancellation, works its way through the remainder of the queue:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Core/Sinks/Batching/BatchingSink.cs#L169

comments.body:
Hi John! Quite a bit to digest there, so just a couple of quick thoughts/answers, others with more Aspire experience might jump in :-)

* For Seq, whether you send events via the Serilog sink or OTEL, I'd recommend using an API key. Allocating different API keys to each unique app and service, per environment, means that you can use Seq's Data > Ingestion page to see how much data is coming from each source, and to filter/restrict it in case of log flooding or noise.
* If you want to see traces in Seq, you'll either need to point an OTLP exporter at it, or wire up SerilogTracing to route activities through the Seq sink.
* OpenTelemetry includes a metrics signal, which neither Serilog nor Seq collect.

HTH,
Nick

Hey @nblumhardt,

Thank you so much for your response. It been a while since we last spoke, and I appreciate you taking the time to address our setup.

Based on your suggestions, I'll make the following adjustments and have a few follow-up questions:

1. API Keys for Seq:

We will implement unique API keys for each app and service per environment. This sounds like an excellent way to manage and monitor our data ingestion. Is there a best practice for managing these keys in an Aspire environment, particularly for local development?

2. Traces in Seq:

We'll explore both options you mentioned. For our use case, which would you recommend:
   a) Pointing an OTLP exporter at Seq, AND
   b) Wiring up SerilogTracing to route activities through the Seq sink?

Are there pros and cons to each approach in an Aspire context? We want to avoid duplication in Seq or the Aspire Console I guess and we tend to lean toward SerilogTracing but would this be reported to the Aspire Console as well ? 

3. OpenTelemetry Metrics:

Thanks for clarifying that about metrics. Given that neither Serilog nor Seq collect these, what would you recommend as a complementary solution for metrics collection that would integrate well with our Serilog/Seq/Aspire stack? Is there anything on the roadmap for Serilog / Seq that would support this ?

4. Aspire Integration:

Since you mentioned others might have more Aspire experience, are there any Aspire-specific considerations we should keep in mind when implementing these changes, particularly regarding the Service Defaults setup? I feel like we have to have our feet in both camps but I'd rather be all in with Serilog and Seq without deliberately breaking or ignoring the Aspire Console functionality unless I really had too.

Again, thank you for your guidance. Your insights have always helped shape our observations and logging strategy.

Best regards,

John

Thanks for the reply, John! Here's my impressions -

On 1, I'd consider logging locally during development and not worrying about an API key at all. `Aspire.Hosting.Seq` can help with spinning up a local Seq container, or you can just log to a local Seq instance and all should be good. If you're writing to a shared development server, then I think this is a case where I wouldn't worry too much about API keys either. The main benefits are in the production context.

For 2, either or both should work. I like the SerilogTracing API considerably more than bare System.Diagnostics.Activity, so I'd lean towards trying to get it in there. There's still the option to go with bare System.Diagnostics.Activity and let traces flow to Seq through the OpenTelemetry SDK and an OTLP exporter if you hit any awkward integration points.

Metrics (3) brings Prometheus to mind, though I haven't used it in a production setting. InfluxDB + Grafana is the combination I have most experience with and enjoyed a lot, but that was many years ago.

Today, internally, we use Seq + an experimental feature flag to ingest OTLP metrics into Seq, and we have some automation which produces dashboards based on metric definitions. It's great to use for our purposes, but we haven't publicised this because the underlying event storage is too inefficient to be competitive for heavy metrics workloads. Our roadmap has native metrics support right at the top, https://datalust.co/roadmap - but given the imminent release of clustering and our expectation that a lot of resources will go into it over the next few months, it's more likely that native OTLP metrics is a 2026 project for us.

On 4, hoping others will chime in, looking forward to learning more about this myself.

Sorry about the slow reply, the week got away on me! Have a good weekend.

When you set up Serilog, you'll somewhere be doing an `AddSerilog()` or `UseSerilog()` call to wire it into MEL, and/or setting `Log.Logger` to an `ILogger` instance.

You may be able to get what you're after by wrapping this root logger in your own custom type, which would need to implement `ILogger`, `IDisposable`, and `IAsyncDisposable`.

All methods would forward to the wrapped logger, except `IsEnabled(LogEventLevel)`, which would perform some custom check based on an `AsyncLocal`, and `ForContext()`, which would use the same logic as `IsEnabled()` to detect that the current request/activity/whatever is a sampled one, and in those cases, wrap the results of calling `ForContext()` on the inner logger in an additional instance of your wrapper type before returning the result.

Hope this helps!
Nick

Hi @AleyCZ! Semi-related - which IoC container are you using? For Autofac, you can use this https://github.com/nblumhardt/autofac-serilog-integration to have the right contextual logger injected without a generic type involved.

I'm open to the idea of supporting this more deeply, though I'm not sure yet how it would fit into the overall design of Serilog. Since this is normally a feature relating to constructor injection, it would be interesting to explore what other options are available with the container you're using.
This would be a nice addition

@nblumhardt would be nice to use this as we make everything a primary constructor.
Just allow Serilog.Ilogger<T> in the same way that MEF.Ilogger<T> works.

I find myself often coming back to this issue, and am surprised it is not getting more traction. Do people not want to use primary constructors? Or are they not injecting Serilog.ILogger? Or are they not enriching the logger with the class? How are people using Serilog along with primary constructors?

I'm probably in the minority, but for me, a class's constructor argument list is precious real estate that I don't really want cluttered up with `ILogger<T>`.

Just like we don't thread through allocators, or `TaskScheduler`, or a million other noisy details of the execution environment, I don't usually like threading through loggers. They're a cross-cutting concern, most of the time, so I'm happier using static state and the `Log` class.

`ILogger<T>` also falls apart when a component needs to call a function or construct another component that needs a logger - but with a different `T`.

YMMV, and I do still end up writing code that uses `ILogger`/`ILogger<T>` injection quite a bit, so I'm not against this on principle or anything like that.

FWIW, the `T` part isn't strictly required, it's also possible to have `ILogger` injected with `ForContext()` called behind the scenes, if your IoC container has the hook points to plug it in: https://github.com/nblumhardt/autofac-serilog-integration

Thanks for the note. This is a change in ASP.NET Core, rather than Serilog - Serilog has always quoted strings in the default message rendering mode.

I'd love to change this - I don't think it'd be out of the question for a Serilog 4.0 - but for now your best bet is to modify the formatter.

One simple, quick solution is to switch to _Serilog.Expressions_ for JSON formatting:

```csharp
    .WriteTo.Console(new ExpressionTemplate(
        "{ {Timestamp: @t, Level: @l, MessageTemplate: @mt, RenderedMessage: @m, Exception: @x, Properties: @p} }\n"))
```

_Serilog.Expressions_ already uses the nicer message rendering that you're after.

If the code is performance-sensitive at this level, you might instead grab the code for `MessageTemplateRenderer` from:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Rendering/MessageTemplateRenderer.cs

and then embed a modified version of `RenderedCompactJsonFormatter` that uses it (with slightly modified structure and field names) into your project:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog-formatting-compact/blob/dev/src/Serilog.Formatting.Compact/Formatting/Compact/RenderedCompactJsonFormatter.cs

HTH,
Nick

comments.body:
I think your second statement:

```
Log.Information("Byte array: {@Data}", [| 1uy |])
```

isn't calling the overload of `Information()` that you're expecting - its first arg is a `params` array.

Let me know if this helps :-)

No, that's not it. Here is a modification to the repro that uses multiple values, thereby avoiding that ambiguity. The output is the same as the original example.

```f#
Log.Information("Byte {Kind}: {@Data}", "list", List([ 1uy ]))
Log.Information("Byte {Kind}: {@Data}", "array", [| 1uy |])
```

🤔 hmmmmmm... I think then it will be that byte arrays are processed as scalars (converted to hex strings):

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Capturing/PropertyValueConverter.cs#L68

but other enumerable types (`FSharp.Core.List`?) don't get that special treatment and pass through:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Capturing/PropertyValueConverter.cs#L174

I don't think it's likely to be a bug per se, just the outcome of different types being processed differently - not sure whether/where we'd make any changes to enable a different approach, but if you're able to share some more info about your scenario/preferences it'd be good data to have. Thanks!

> `FSharp.Core.List`?

The repro uses `System.Collections.Generic.List` (typically aliased as `ResizeArray` in F#), though that's irrelevant. The only requirement is that it is not an array.

> if you're able to share some more info about your scenario/preferences it'd be good data to have.

Certainly!

Destructuring _per se_  doesn't help me, so I don't use that. In fact, it would actively hurt me, at least in the first case below.
- A lot of my logging goes to Application Insights, and I really don't want to duplicate big objects between log messages and properties (which significantly increases ingestion costs). In fact, I have a custom wrapper sink for Application Insights that (while preserving the message template itself) replaces the tokens in the message with the rendered values, thereby only sending the final rendered message and the message template to AI, and not any of the message tokens as separate properties.
- A lot of my other logging is done on edge/IoT devices where I log to syslog/logcat but (for data usage reasons) do not transfer the logs out of the device at all (except when there's a problem and I sign into the device to check the logs). Destructuring is pointless here; only the rendered message is shown.

In both of these cases, the only thing that matter to me is the log message. I therefore simply want the rendered log message to be as nicely formatted as possible.

To achieve this, I am serializing most values using custom settings, so they are easy to read. (I used JSON first, but recently switched to YAML because it's even easier to read.)

I use this not only for complex objects, but also single-case discriminated unions ("wrapped primitives"), which are unwrapped using my serialization settings. In general, no matter what I serialize using my "log JSON setting", the output is either better or the same, never worse.

Of course, relative to other performance costs of logging, serialization is a heavy hitter. I used to serialize synchronously and insert the string directly into the log message (`Log.Information("Foo {Bar}", logSerialize myObject)`), but this is wasteful if the log level is not enabled (and in many cases, I logged complex objects at a normally disabled log level). I found out that I could make use of a custom destructuring policy and instead use the destructure operator `@`, which meant that the objects would not be serialized if the log level was not enabled. Also, it's less verbose. So (`Log.Information("Foo {@Bar}", myObject)` would be equivalent to the previous statement, but only serialize if the log level was enabled.

I have not found any other way to accomplish 1) nice custom-formatted complex objects in log messages, and 2) not serializing for disabled log levels.

In terms of this issue, the point is that this destructuring-based approach works wonderfully for everything except byte arrays. Specifically, I'd like to represent them with spaces between the bytes, like `FA 2E C9`, because that makes it easier for me to know "what is byte 5", and easier to paste into other tools we use that accept this format. For byte lists and other byte sequences, it works fine, but the different handling of byte arrays means it didn't work there. This was surprising to me, because there is not just one accepted way to render byte arrays.

Thanks for taking the time to write that! 👍 

I've never been entirely comfortable with our opinionated byte array formatting - the current system came about though because treating byte arrays as lists of bytes was ...... problematic to say the least 😅 ... so something (useful) needed to be done.

Unfortunately, byte arrays are something of an anomaly; most/all "scalar" types Serilog cares about are structs/value objects, which have copy semantics and so can be passed as-is through to the asynchronous side of the logging pipeline, or in the case of `string`, are immutable. Because of this there isn't a great extension point for dealing with byte arrays.

In the past we've considered making `IScalarConversionPolicy` a public/pluggable extension point, along the same lines as `IDestructuringPolicy`, which would potentially sort out your scenario, but it's a nontrival bit of infrastructure to design and maintain without a broadly-relevant set of use cases. This could be something to explore more deeply but probably requires quite a lot of effort.

Depending on how much control you have on the application side, constructing a proxy type such as:

```csharp
record struct ByteArrayProxy(byte[] Bytes);

Log.Information("Some {Data}", new ByteArrayProxy(myBytes));
```

and then targeting it with an `IDestructuringPolicy` would be a possible workaround. (Forgive the C# syntax :-))

Hope this helps.

Thanks for the clarification!

I am indeed wrapping the byte array as a workaround (in the `Some` case of F#'s `option` type, which using my serialization settings is unwrapped).

In any case, what I really want is to be able to control how Serilog formats values of arbitrary types. The fact that I'm using destructuring is just because that's the only way I found. If it would be possible to add a way to let users specify formatting of arbitrary types (e.g., pass `obj` and let the user decide how to transform/stringify it), then that would solve my problem in a less hacky way, would allow me to use destructuring for actual destructuring (if I ever need that), and would also mean I don't have to remember to use `@` everywhere (easy to forget, leading to bad output, and I don't see that before I actually see an example of the relevant log message, which is in some ways the worst kind of error).

The reason to use destructuring or enrichment is that Serilog does capturing on the foreground thread (at the point the event is logged), but formatting on a (potentially) background thread. By the time the data reaches the formatting stage it's already been snapshotted; this is how mutable things like arrays end up logged with the right contents (and race conditions/threading bugs are avoided). HTH!
Thanks, though I'm not sure what you intend for me to do with that information?
Just filling in the picture, unfortunately it doesn't get us closer to a solution, just narrows down the possible places to investigate :-)

title: Top-level byte array isn't destructured, but other byte sequences are

Are the developers here open to this suggestion? And if so, can we help in any way?

Hi @ProximaB and @Corniel,

I've been working on a Go port of Serilog called [mtlog](https://github.com/willibrandon/mtlog) with an accompanying analyzer. While it's for a different language, our [mtlog-analyzer](https://github.com/willibrandon/mtlog/tree/main/cmd/mtlog-analyzer) experience might offer useful insights for a Roslyn analyzer.

**Key features that proved essential:**
- **Automatic fixes** - Property naming conventions, constant extraction, argument count corrections
- **Severity levels** - Errors (breaking), warnings (likely mistakes), suggestions (best practices)  
- **IDE integration** - Real-time validation significantly improves developer experience
- **Flexible suppression** - Kill switch for all diagnostics or suppress individual warnings as needed
- **Gradual adoption** - Configurable checks and severity downgrading for legacy codebases

**Common issues our analyzer catches:**
```go
// ❌ Template/argument mismatch
log.Information("User {UserId} logged in from {IP}", userId)

// ❌ Duplicate properties
log.Information("User {UserId} did {Action} as {UserId}", id, "login", id)

// ⚠️ Repeated string literals → suggests constants
log.ForContext("user_id", 123).Information("Login")
// Quick fix: const userIDKey = "user_id"

// 💡 Complex types without capturing hints
log.Information("User: {User}", user)
// Suggests: {@User} or implementing LogValue()
```

The analyzer has been invaluable for catching template errors at compile time and enforcing consistent logging practices. Happy to share more implementation details if helpful.

The referenced implementation for Roslyn gives you most of that, and I'm am willing to do the implementation. But a nuget package has to be created, documentation pages to be hosted (explaining the rule violations) That is stuff I most likely do not have the rights for.

I can't speak for that, but if there is anything I can do to help with design, or testing, please let me know. I've been diving deep into Serilog related editor integrations lately and these topic are very interesting to me.

title: Official Roslyn analyzer based on Suchiman/SerilogAnalyzer work

Agree. This is a common problem of design with an implicit configuration of sinks from configuration. As I understand Graylog repository **may** provide needed overload accepting delegate to set `Func<ITransport> TransportFactory` but it will not help in case of using `ReadFrom.Configuration(configuration)`. I should note that configuration subsystem of Serilog supports some non-trivial features like constructing delegates so with some effort you **may** achive your goal but I agree that this it is not convenient to do and personally I would not.

Also note that sinks are often considered to be immutable after creating. You provided `Func<ITransport> TransportFactory` property that exists on options object passed into Graylog sink. `GraylogSink` **may** use this options object only in ctor so further modification of it does nothing.

I propose to add special API for one-time sinks configuration. See #1930. @nblumhardt If OK I'm glag to discuss naming and other details.

Of course, more changes are needed in the Graylog repository because as you say, once the options is instantiated and the sink constructor is called, it is not possible to change any settings:

https://github.com/serilog-contrib/serilog-sinks-graylog/blob/590183d1b0d04d0d05eaa50c0a3b1d7c2d4daab3/src/Serilog.Sinks.Graylog/LoggerConfigurationGrayLogExtensions.cs#L47

But I didn't want to create noise on this issue because it is a concrete problem of that Graylog extension implementation on Serilog.

@bdovaz please don't @ anyone in an issue like this.
This repo has tonnes of watchers and contributors.
If someone is a watcher, they'll get there in their own good time.
This is the only way someone (and the associated contributors, of which there are quite a few for Serilog) can magically do day jobs while also serving this amount of happy customers per 6 weeks: https://www.nuget.org/stats/packages/Serilog?groupby=Version
(I do get that you are also a contributor, and meant no harm. I'm also not suggesting that you're doing this persistently. Just that you can't be too thoughtful when raising issues on a project like this, regardless how of how much you'd value a specific person's perspective. The exception is if you were specifically asked by the person in question to @ them when it's logged in the case of some pre-discussion)

>  it is a concrete problem of that Graylog extension implementation on Serilog.

I understand and exactly because of that I suggested generic API to configure any sink regardless of its implementation capabilities. One-time setup is important thing for me in terms of overall design. I would not expose some list of sinks from configuration object.

> >  it is a concrete problem of that Graylog extension implementation on Serilog.
> 
> I understand and exactly because of that I suggested generic API to configure any sink regardless of its implementation capabilities. One-time setup is important thing for me in terms of overall design. I would not expose some list of sinks from configuration object.

What I meant (and maybe I was misunderstood) with that sentence is that even if we have exposed your new API design (which I think is great) is that if you look at how the graylog sink consumes the options class, it is too late to change properties of the configuration instance.

In that specific sink more changes are needed and we would have to analyze extension by extension if we have to change the design of each one so that this is possible in all of them. Because there is no common pattern of options + sink.

The ideal pattern of options classes is Microsoft's IOptions<> but I understand that you don't want to have a hard dependency on the Serilog core towards Microsoft extensions.

Hi all! Sorry about the patchy availability here, I'm taking a short break and only jumping online sporadically. Back to full speed late next week.

This sounds like a problem unique to _Serilog.Settings.Configuration_, to me. Using some kind of static factory method or constructor should enable this without too much additional machinery. It's slightly awkward, but it's also a fairly niche scenario.

The other solution, which I personally prefer, is to just configure the sink in code, and pull the dynamically-varied configuration from your own custom configuration section (probably just a couple of flat values that identify the Graylog endpoint). Simple and reliable :-)

>   if you look at how the graylog sink consumes the options class, it is too late to change properties of the configuration instance.

I 100% understand that and already told about that particular case. Serilog code _may_ expose suggested new APIs to configure sinks in **any** way sink **supports**.

>  is to just configure the sink in code

Or couse, but the more interesting question is about how to provide additional tuning when starting entirely from `ReadFrom.Configuration`. In my practice I have always configured such sinks from code.

Pros and in the same time cons of suggested `ConfigurationReaderOptions.OnSinkCreated` design is that it works only for sinks constructed from that configuration API. But what is more important is that you still have no access to created sink. You can not write such API because configuration project does not create sinks explicitly, it calls extension methods which add sinks, see `ApplySinks` method from configuration repo.

I'm happy leaving this discussion open if it might flush out some workable solution, but I feel like direct access to sinks goes against the grain of the Serilog design, which deliberately hides them so that sinks can be implemented using techniques like wrapping, which would get in the way of this kind of usage.

Take for example the way `Serilog.Sinks.Async`, `Serilog.Sinks.PeriodicBatching`, or `Serilog.Sinks.Map` work - in those cases the actual type of the sink added to the logging pipeline isn't the one you might expect, and there's no single/sensible way to get at an "inner sink" in those cases, since the inner thing might not even be a sink itself (the periodic batching case) or might be created deep inside a separate piece of infrastructure (the map case).

For these reasons I think it's a ship that has sailed. There are definitely other ways Serilog could approach this, with various pros and cons, but because a design has been chosen I think a solution would need to embrace the decisions that have already been made.

Since _Serilog.Settings.Configuration_ is calling those sink creation extension methods, perhaps instead of looking to access the raw sink, an extension point could be created there for resolving parameters to the extension method?

E.g. `OnCollectSinkArgs(string sinkName, IDictionary<string, object?> args)`? (Likely to itself require some design of course :-))

Hope this helps,
Nick
Just for information - I updated proposal in #1930 with the latest changes  from `dev`.

This sounds good to me.

The scenario might not warrant the addition of the _Microsoft.Bcl.TimeProvider_ dependency on downlevel platforms, since adopters of `TimeProvider` are more than likely going to be targeting .NET 8 anyway - ?

It might be worth running over any other possible `TimeProvider` integration points; `PeriodicBatchingSink` is the one that comes to mind, though `TimeProvider` use there would be almost entirely ours (I can't imagine too many people unit testing batched sinks in that manner 🤔).

I would not touching `Microsoft.Bcl.TimeProvider`. I would add serilog's own time abstraction (like `TimeProvider` one but interface and with single method) and pass it into internal Logger ctor. Abstraction can be configured/set via fluent builder.

> I would not touching `Microsoft.Bcl.TimeProvider`.

Proposal 1. doesn't touch it, only targets .NET 8.

> I would add serilog's own time abstraction (like `TimeProvider` one but interface and with single method).

Why? The [Standards](https://xkcd.com/927/) xkcd comes to mind. 😉

![Fortunately, the charging one has been solved now that we've all standardized on mini-USB. Or is it micro-USB? Shit.](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/assets/51363/7e740de0-70f1-4701-bbbd-524607ab8740)

Now that's it's available in .NET 8 I expect people will start adopting it instead of rolling their own.

RE the API, I suspect using the fluent syntax might avoid some situations where we end up with parallel constructors needed in order to keep passing along a time provider 🤔 (which gets nastier if conditional compilation is required).

There's a bit of precedent for modifying how events are captured in the way message template parameters are bound - perhaps we should think about revising `ILogEventPropertyFactory` etc. to include more general "capturing" concepts like the time provider?

I'm not set one way or the other on the BCL package dependency; conditional dependencies are a pain, but conditional compilation is at least as bad; since within a few years practically every active .NET project will have some dependency on `TimeProvider`, and a substantial chunk of those will use their local framework copy, I'd be inclined towards the package dependency, which will naturally age out once the platforms requiring it are retired (as opposed to conditional compilation, which needs to be manually pulled out of the codebase).

> Why? The [Standards](https://xkcd.com/927/) xkcd comes to mind.

Not applicable. It not about standards, it's about dependencies - either direct from package (bad, Serilog have always been against it) or indirect via interfaces.

Shall we dig in a bit deeper assuming that we'll either conditionally target .NET 8, or conditionally reference the package on earlier platforms? We can get a feel for the impacts of each once we've traced through all the implications.

I don't think we should define our own interfaces here if we can avoid it - there's not much point if they'll be obsoleted within a few years by the built-in abstractions, and we might end up wanting to take deeper dependencies on `TimeProvider` features like sleeps and so-on, later down the track, which would be harder if we have our own abstractions to extend.

Hey folks, hope you're all well. Just a tiny note, #2120 needed a clock abstraction for testing, so I tried to find a happy medium between "NIH" and "more new dependencies". There's now a very minimal `TimeProvider` polyfill in `Util/TimeProvider.cs`, which we use on .NET versions without it, and on `net8.0` we just use the real thing.

As of that change, time providers are only usable in tests/internal APIs, not public ones. This might be a nice way for us to build up a plan and internal support for time providers right away, and defer making a call on how to inject them until we actually have some functionality there to justify it.

(It's also possible a `SetTimeProvider()` sort of API could be conditionally available on `net8.0`+ only, side-stepping the dependency issue and making the internal polyfill solution a long-term fix?)

comments.body:
Thanks for the suggestion! The current design of `SelfLog` assumes that it's only turned on when trying to diagnose a problem; although a lot of people do use it for monitoring, there are some gaps to fill before this would be a good experience.

I don't think we're aiming to create a mini logging framework around `SelfLog`, so I'd personally be inclined to leave this alone. Open to hearing other perspectives though.

I understand it would be a logger inside logger, but I think changes would be really minor and worth benefits.
Its just matter of adding log level enum and pass it around two methods.

Logger inside logger, yes, but not so complicated logger. I would say very primitive logger. I agree that changes should be minimal but they are likely breaking. I would add new `SelfLog`-like property and some switch to use either old `SelfLog` or the new one (+ optionally deprecate old `SelfLog`).

> I would add new SelfLog-like property and some switch to use either old SelfLog or the new one (+ optionally deprecate old SelfLog).

In my opinion it would be "more breaking" and complicating the solution.
Simply adding log level is also breaking, but fixing it is very simple and obvious - it is just matter of setting appropriate log level for all WriteLine methods - the compiler will not pass missing parameter.

Another quicker and more efficient option might be to just send PRs to the two projects listed in the original report for a conditional "verbose diagnostics" switch - worth serious consideration, since landing changes in two sinks will be much faster and more effective than trying to land changes in the hundreds of others already written.

> landing changes in two sinks will be much faster and more effective than trying to land changes in the hundreds of others already written

And hundreds of already written would still use selflog improperly. This fix would make it clear how to use selflog. And adapting to new requirements would be really easy for those libraries.
SelfLog is only really intended to be switched on when you're diagnosing a problem, so the current usage is probably correct across the board, to be fair.

At risk of branching out the discussion, I'm seeing a need for both Level and more context, such as the exception, the logger type/name and ideally any additional properties the SelfLog writer wants to include. Similar to a standard log event really.

### Why
We notify ourselves on Slack on SelfLog events, so we can be aware of logging issues.

This is currently a bit spammy and additional context would help us filter spam and provide more details for diagnostics:
- There is no context about the class that had problems or the severity of the problem. We need to use regex to filter out messages we can't do anything about.
- There is no exception details, which would help diagnose the sink if it was related to say JSON serialization exception, HTTP request or writing to disk.
- Additional context, for example [Serilog.Sinks.Logz.Io](https://github.com/serilog-contrib/Serilog.Sinks.Logz.Io) sometimes report 403 Bad Request on SelfLog. It would be possible for the sink to include information about the HTTP request and response in this case, if this is not already made available via the exception.


### Example of SelfLog event that could be Info/Warn level

I'm not sure if this is a bug in the sink configuration, or if this is a common scenario that should be Info/Warn level and could be ignored.

We get this log event twice from SelfLog on startup when using [Serilog.Sinks.ApplicationInsights](https://github.com/serilog-contrib/serilog-sinks-applicationinsights).

```
2023-03-28T08:07:23.0821036Z Ignoring added logger provider Microsoft.ApplicationInsights.AspNetCore.Logging.ApplicationInsightsLoggerProvider
2023-03-28T08:07:23.1435203Z Ignoring added logger provider Microsoft.ApplicationInsights.AspNetCore.Logging.ApplicationInsightsLoggerProvider
```

From what I can tell, this sink is trying to add a Microsoft logger provider and `SerilogLoggerFactory` warns about ignoring this, since I assume it would result in duplicate log events when using `UseSerilog()`.

https://github.com/serilog/serilog-aspnetcore/blob/bf4ae072f7472d285c72f9a43f3eb4920e743110/src/Serilog.AspNetCore/AspNetCore/SerilogLoggerFactory.cs#L63-L70

```cs
    /// <summary>
    /// Adds an <see cref="T:Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.ILoggerProvider" /> to the logging system.
    /// </summary>
    /// <param name="provider">The <see cref="T:Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.ILoggerProvider" />.</param>
    public void AddProvider(ILoggerProvider provider)
    {
        SelfLog.WriteLine("Ignoring added logger provider {0}", provider);
    }
```

### Proposal: New SelfLog.Write methods and new SelfLog.OnEvent callback

The new methods would be opt-in and the old methods backwards compatible.

- Add type `SelfLogEvent`, a simpler variant of `LogEvent` without templating and where property dictionary is `object` instead of `LogEventPropertyValue` to not support rendering of values.
- Add `SelfLog.Write` methods similar to `Serilog.ILogger.Write`, without templating and where properties must be explicitly specified - no ambient context.
  -  `SelfLog.Write(SelfLogEvent)`
  -  `SelfLog.Write(LogEventLevel, string message, Type? source)`
  -  `SelfLog.Write(LogEventLevel, Exception?, string message, Type? source)`
  -  `SelfLog.Write(LogEventLevel, Exception?, string message, Type? source, IDictionary<string, object>?)`
- Add `SelfLog.OnEvent` method with callback that includes the additional properties in a `SelfLogEvent` type.
- `SelfLog.WriteLine` writes to `SelfLog.Write` with `Error` level and `null` for the other values.
- `SelfLog.Write` invokes both `SelfLog.OnEvent` and `SelfLog.Enable` callbacks, backwards compatible.
- Obsolete `SelfLog.WriteLine`, instruct to use new overload
- Obsolete `SelfLog.Enable`, instruct to use new overload


### Related issues

An open PR proposes to include the exception details if a log event fails, but this would not include any exceptions inside the sink itself:
#1651

Good ideas - in the past I've had a desire to be able to flag Async Sink buffer overflows (i.e. notifying when events were being jetissoned) too - we had Async emission to a File sink, and >= error emission to the console (that would egress via k8s/nomad host). The Console sink was assumed to be failsafe, so warnings from other sinks were routed there.

Something like what you outlined ☝️ might allow the Async Sink to emit notifications OOTB which you can then wire to a failsafe sink (vs having to handwire it via the notiification APIs I added, which I trust have very low usage levels system wide). The PeriodicBatching Sink also has relatively similar needs. Any reboot of the Async Sink based on Channels should also be considered in such a design.

@nblumhardt Wouldn't it be just another SelfLog but different way? Just like adding a few new arguments to SelfLog. How will it prevent from misusing SelfLog? In my opinion there should be a single, good solution for selflogging instead of two solutions. This will lead to misunderstanding.

The difference in thinking is might be that to me there _is_ a single good solution for self-logging, it's just not the feature you were originally looking for. SelfLog really is just intended to be turned on when a problem has to be debugged, it's not supposed to be collected and acted on in production scenarios, despite it being possible to do so.

SelfLog isn't just lacking the `level` argument, it's got no actionable semantics at all, except for "here's something you might look at if logging isn't working for you". Exceptions propagate from SelfLog subscribers; there's no system of sinks not susceptible to recursion/stack overflow, etc.

Delivery monitoring and failover is often requested without any mention of SelfLog, but when you dig into both kinds of requests - failing over to secondary sinks, or being alerted when logging fails, and a more complex SelfLog - there's a common thread that's worth exploring.

Hi everyone! For anyone still tracking this, I've spiked out #2018, which introduces:

```csharp
public interface ILoggingFailureListener
{
    void OnLoggingFailed(
        object sender,
        LoggingFailureKind kind,
        string message,
        IReadOnlyCollection<LogEvent>? events,
        Exception? exception);
}
```

I don't think it came out too badly; I think the information provided to listeners will cover just about everything in this thread, including making failures clear and distinct from "information" messages, writing events to fallback sinks, and because failure listeners are configured per-sink, there's no danger of "fallback inception" if the listener wants to forward events on through another Serilog pipeline.

Feedback and ideas welcome!
